essence: Track the streak, and never miss twice in a row.
modern_lens: Chapter 16 offers simple tools to keep habits going: a visual tracker, the rule never to miss twice, and a warning about measuring the wrong thing. Teams and individuals both benefit from seeing progress, and from a plan for bad days that keeps the routine alive.

ideas.name: Track the Habit
ideas.text: A habit tracker, such as a calendar where you cross off each day, makes progress obvious, attractive and satisfying. It works as a cue, a motivator and an instant reward. Mark it immediately after the behaviour so the record stays honest.
ideas.try: Draw a 30-day grid for one habit and put it where you will see it daily.

ideas.name: Do Not Break the Chain
ideas.text: A visible streak becomes its own motivation. Seeing a run of completed days makes you reluctant to end it. Keep the measure simple enough to mark in a few seconds.
ideas.try: Track only one yes-or-no question for a habit, such as: did I start today?

ideas.name: Never Miss Twice
ideas.text: Missing one day is an accident; missing two is the start of a new habit. When life gets in the way, get back on track at the next chance, even with a tiny version. The first miss is never the problem; the slide after it is.
ideas.try: Write your minimum version for bad days now, so a miss is never followed by another.

ideas.name: Measure the Right Thing
ideas.text: When a measure becomes the target, people optimise the number instead of the goal: tickets closed quickly instead of problems solved, kilograms on the scale instead of health. Use numbers as feedback, and keep the purpose in view.
ideas.try: For one metric you track, write the real goal next to it and check they still match.

ideas.name: Bad Days Still Count
ideas.text: Showing up at reduced intensity on a bad day protects the habit. A ten-minute workout or a two-line journal entry keeps your identity intact. On a bad day the goal is to keep the routine alive, not to perform.
ideas.try: Define the smallest version of your habit that still counts, and use it on your next bad day.
